posts.title: Is someone already inside your phone?
posts.listDesc: The 5-minute check that tells you for sure — session lists, unknown devices, and what to do if you find something.
posts.intro: Right now, on the exact phone in your hand, there could be a device logged into your account that isn't yours. Maybe there isn't — but you don't actually know, because most people never check. This is the real 5-minute check, not a hypothetical: no app to install, nothing to buy, just open a settings menu and look.
posts.statLine: $ context — 292 days. That's the average time it takes someone to realize their login was stolen, according to IBM. Nearly a year of someone else quietly having access, before anyone notices.

paragraphs: Open Settings → [your name] → Password Options → Security Recommendations, or just scroll down from Settings → [your name] — either way, you'll see the full list of every device currently signed into your Apple ID. Every single one.
Open the Google app → Profile picture → Manage your Google Account → Security → Your devices — this is the full guest list for your Google account, every device currently signed in.
Scan it slowly. A device model you've never owned. A city you've never set foot in. A login time you can't place. Any one of those is worth stopping on.

sections.title: Look for apps you didn't install

paragraphs: Scroll through your full app list — not just your home screen, the real list under Settings → Apps. Spyware doesn't usually announce itself; it hides behind boring, forgettable names like "System Update," "Device Health," or "Battery Optimizer."
If you can't remember installing something and can't explain what it does, don't shrug it off. That's exactly the gap it's counting on.

sections.title: Check for a profile you didn't set up

paragraphs: Go to Settings → General → VPN & Device Management. A configuration profile is normal on a work phone — someone in IT put it there on purpose. On your personal phone, one you don't remember installing means someone else may have remote access to it. That's not routine, that's a red flag.

Go to Settings → Security → Device admin apps. Anything sitting here that you didn't knowingly turn on — an unfamiliar "Find My Device"-style app, for instance — deserves a second look before you move on.

sections.title: Run your phone's built-in security checkup

paragraphs: Both Google and Apple already built the easy version of this for you — Google Account → Security → Security Checkup, or the Security Recommendations screen from Step 1 on iPhone. One tap, and it flags weak passwords, reused passwords, and sign-ins you don't recognize automatically.

quiz.question: Have you checked which devices are logged into your phone or accounts in the last 6 months?

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU FIND SOMETHING
warn.text: Don't panic, but do act. Sign out of any device you don't recognize immediately, change your password from a device you trust (not the compromised one), and turn on two-factor authentication if it isn't already on. If it looks like stalkerware specifically, consider that removing it may alert whoever installed it — if this is a safety concern involving another person, that's worth thinking through carefully before you act.

checklist: Checked which devices are logged into your Apple ID / Google account
Scanned your full app list for anything unfamiliar
Checked for configuration profiles / device admin apps you didn't set up

posts.title: The password mistake nobody thinks is a big deal
posts.listDesc: Why reusing one password anywhere is worse than you think, and how a password manager actually fixes it.
posts.intro: Here's the spoiler: it's reusing the same password on more than one site. It feels completely harmless — until it's the reason your email, your bank, and half your other accounts all get hit on the same afternoon.
posts.statLine: $ context — one password, leaked from any random site you signed up for years ago, can unlock every other account where you reused it. It's called credential stuffing, and a machine does it in seconds, not a person.

sections.title: See if you've actually done this

paragraphs: Go to passwords.google.com or Settings → Password Manager → Password Checkup and let it do the uncomfortable part for you — it'll show you exactly which passwords are reused, weak, or already sitting in a known breach.
Go to Settings → Passwords → Security Recommendations. Same idea — it flags reused and compromised passwords for you automatically.
Most people are surprised by how long that list is. That's normal, not a sign you did anything unusually careless — this is just what everyone's list looks like before they check.

bad.label: ✕ ONE PASSWORD, EVERYWHERE
bad.text: One site gets breached — maybe one you signed up for once and forgot about. Your email and password leak together. Within seconds, automated tools are trying that exact combo on hundreds of other sites: banking, email, social media.

good.label: ✓ UNIQUE PER SITE
good.text: That same site gets breached. But the leaked password is useless anywhere else, because it was never used anywhere else. The damage stops at one account instead of spreading through your entire digital life.

sections.title: Set up a password manager (it's easier than remembering)

paragraphs: Good news: you don't have to memorize unique passwords for every account — a password manager remembers them for you. Your phone almost certainly already has one built in, for free: iCloud Keychain on iPhone, or Google Password Manager on Android/Chrome.
Want one that works identically no matter what device or browser you're on? Bitwarden is free and widely trusted. Either path is a genuine upgrade over trying to remember it all yourself.

sections.title: Fix your most important accounts first

paragraphs: You don't need to fix every account today — that's how people give up halfway through. Start with the ones that would hurt most if compromised: your primary email (it can reset almost everything else), your banking apps, and anything with saved payment info.
Let the password manager generate a new, unique password for each one as you go, and just keep chipping away at the rest over time.

warn.label: ⚠ IF A PASSWORD SHOWS UP AS "COMPROMISED"
warn.text: Change it immediately, starting with that account and anywhere else you used the same one. If it's your email password specifically, treat it as urgent — email is usually the master key to everything else you own online.

checklist: Ran a password checkup to see what's reused or compromised
Turned on your phone's built-in password manager
Fixed email, banking, and payment-linked accounts first
Let the manager generate unique passwords going forward

posts.title: What is smishing?
posts.listDesc: The exact texts scammers send, why they work, and how to tell a real message from a fake one in seconds.
posts.intro: Smishing is just SMS phishing — a scam text engineered to look official enough that you click before your brain catches up. The wording changes every time. The pattern underneath almost never does, and once you can see it, these texts stop working on you.
posts.statLine: $ context — smishing works because a text feels more urgent and more "official" than an email ever does, and almost nobody's ever been taught to question one.

sections.title: The pattern, not the exact words

paragraphs: Almost every smishing text is built from the same three ingredients: a name you trust (your bank, a delivery company, the tax office), a problem that supposedly needs fixing right now, and a link that promises to fix it. Swap the wording and it's a new scam — the structure underneath is always the same.

items.text: A package supposedly couldn't be delivered — click the link to pay a small fee or "confirm" your address.
Suspicious activity on your account, apparently — click through and "verify" by logging in on their page, not yours.
You've supposedly won something, and the countdown clock in the text wants you to "claim" it before you have time to think.

sections.title: Check the sender, not just the message

paragraphs: Real companies text from consistent, verifiable numbers or short codes — the same one, message after message. Scam texts tend to come from a random-looking mobile number, an email-style address, or a number that's different every single time.
When in doubt, scroll back to a past message from that company and compare. Does the number actually match?

sections.title: Never tap the link — go direct instead

paragraphs: Don't tap the link — not even just to look. Open the company's official app instead, or type in their website address yourself, from memory. If something's genuinely wrong with your account or your delivery, it'll be sitting right there too, no scam link required.

sections.title: Notice the urgency — it's the biggest tell

paragraphs: "Act now." "Your account will be suspended." "Offer expires in 1 hour." That urgency isn't accidental — it's the scammer doing their own job for them, engineered to make you click before you've had a chance to think. Real companies almost never demand instant action over text.

quiz.question: When you get a text claiming there's a "delivery problem," what do you do?
quiz.safeLabel: Check the official app or site instead

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU'VE ALREADY CLICKED
warn.text: Don't enter anything if a page asks for a password, card number, or OTP — close it immediately. If you already entered something, change that password right away and check your bank/card statements for anything unfamiliar over the next few days.

checklist: Checked whether the sender number matches past legitimate messages
Didn't tap the link — went to the official app/site directly instead
Noticed the manufactured urgency for what it was
Knows what to do if a link was already tapped
